catalog_quote: Baca has a two-tone system underlyingly, high and low. Contour tones are caused by glide formation from syllable mergers and by the historical reduction from disyllabic to monosyllabic roots. Unlike in some of the other Mbam languages, there is no indication of a loss of contrast of tone melodies in utterance-final position in connection with vowel devoicing or elision. [...] Surface tone is marked on the data in this study. 2.10.5.1 Tone melodies on nouns. High, low, rising and falling melodies contrast in monosyllabic noun roots. In CV, CVC and CVCV noun roots, all four tone melodies are attested, see Example 300 below. Noun prefixes usually have a low tone, although there are a few exceptions. new_statements.rule_in_words: Baca/Nubaca is described as a two-tone (H, L) language with lexical tone melodies on noun and verb roots and rightward H spread in verb stems; the source makes no statement at all about word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; tonal details only (HL vs H verb-melody contrast neutralised before a single non -an suffix).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical (root) tone melodies in citation forms; grammatical tone said to be beyond the scope of the study. Data from the main dialect of Ganok quarter, Bongo village.
new_statements.identity_note: Boyd 2015 describes the main Baca dialect of Ganok quarter, Bongo village (Nubaca [baf] = nuba1241; other dialects Kelende and Nibieg not described). Beware Glottolog's nuba1241 bibliography: Hallowes 1942 'A grammar of Baca' and the Hammond-Tooke items concern Bhaca (Nguni, South Africa), and Paulian 1986 'nukalonge' concerns Yangben [yav]; none of these is a Nubaca source.

sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 2.10 'Baca phonological overview' (pp. 201-222) covers consonants, vowels, vowel harmony, hiatus resolution and tone; sec. 2.10.5 Tone (pp. 220-222): two underlying tones H and L, contour tones from syllable merger/root reduction, H/L/HL/LH noun melodies, L/HL/H verb melodies with H spread. The words stress/accent occur only in a quoted Dixon & Aikhenvald definition (p. 257).

Bibliographic check only: the list is contaminated with works on Bhaca (Nguni, South Africa: Hallowes 1942 'A grammar of Baca', Hammond-Tooke 1953ff.) and Paulian 1986 'nukalonge' (= Yangben [yav]); these are not Nubaca sources.
